solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Miserable, bitter line recalled Milton’s work (7)

indicatorNotes.recalled: to recall is to call back, so the string runs backwards

annotation.surface: A critic dismisses a gloomy, sour line from one of Milton's poems.
annotation.walkthrough: SAD ICY L, read backwards, gives the title. The surface invites you to hunt for a Milton line, when the whole of Milton is only the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Lycidas is Milton's 1637 pastoral elegy for a drowned friend.

entries.clue: Position certainly lowering one’s spare time (7)

indicatorNotes.lowering one’s: in a down entry, lowering the I (one) moves it further down, from LIE to LEI

blocks.note: lie = position (the lie of the land), with its I (one) lowered below the E

annotation.surface: Someone's post, a secure one, is eating into their free time.
annotation.walkthrough: Written for a down entry, where 'lowering' a letter literally moves it further down the grid; one is I, a standard swap.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: leisure is the time left over when work is done.

entries.clue: Sore toe treated with cream initially and antiseptic (8)

indicatorNotes.treated: treated material is worked on and changed, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.initially: takes the first letter of cream

blocks.note: first letter of cream, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A sore toe is dressed with cream and antiseptic.
annotation.walkthrough: The medical picture is apt: creosote from wood tar was once used as an antiseptic, though most readers know it as fence preservative.
annotation.definitionFit: Wood-tar creosote was used medicinally as an antiseptic and expectorant.

entries.clue: Trap caught shape-shifting individuals (5)

indicatorNotes.caught: to catch what someone says is to hear it

blocks.note: a gin is a snare or trap

annotation.surface: Someone snares a set of creatures that can change shape.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like part of the trapping story, or the cricket C; here it means heard. Djinn is plural, matching 'individuals'.
annotation.definitionFit: Djinn are spirits of Islamic lore that can take human or animal form.

entries.clue: Leakage of confidential item carrying charge (9)

blocks.note: the secret carries the charge behind it
an ion is a charged particle

annotation.surface: A classified document is leaked with criminal charges attached.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about a leaked secret; the definition means oozing, as from a gland.
annotation.definitionFit: A secretion is a substance discharged or oozed from a gland or cell.

entries.clue: Acknowledge authenticity of scholarship? (5)

blocks.note: to concede that something is true
money awarded to fund a student

annotation.surface: An academic asks whether a piece of research is genuine.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'scholarship' means money for study, not learning.
annotation.definitionFit: To grant is to admit something as true; a grant is an award of money for study.

entries.clue: In chess, perhaps, manoeuvre ultimately surrendering piece? (6)

annotation.definition: In chess, perhaps, manoeuvre ultimately surrendering piece?

indicatorNotes.perhaps: chess is one example of a game
indicatorNotes.ultimately surrendering: the game gives up its last letter

blocks.note: GAME, an example of which is chess, losing its final E

annotation.surface: A chess player makes an opening move that gives away a piece.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and the wordplay runs through it: GAME surrenders its last letter, then BIT. 'Manoeuvre' serves only the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A gambit is a chess opening in which a pawn or piece is sacrificed for advantage.

entries.clue: One more for each, except this woman (7)

blocks.note: a = per, as in five pounds a head
everyone not her = everyone except her

annotation.surface: Everyone gets a second helping, except one woman left out.
annotation.walkthrough: The small words do the work: 'for each' is A, as in a pound a pint, and 'except this woman' is NOT HER.
annotation.definitionFit: Another means one more of the same kind.

entries.clue: Article based on paper is plagiarism? (5)

indicatorNotes.based on: in a down entry, one piece sits on top of the other

annotation.surface: A journalist asks whether an article copied from a paper counts as plagiarism.
annotation.walkthrough: The Financial Times is a British business daily printed on pink paper; in a down clue 'based on' means sitting on top.
annotation.definitionFit: Plagiarism is the theft of someone else's words or ideas.

entries.clue: Mock article fitting for Men Only (8)

blocks.note: an article is a piece of writing

annotation.surface: A spoof article written for a men's magazine.
annotation.walkthrough: Men Only was a British men's magazine, so the surface reads as a spoof feature. 'Fitting' is a noun here, an accessory, and this one only fits men.
annotation.definitionFit: A codpiece is a pouch covering the crotch on men's hose, so it is a fitting only a man can wear.

entries.clue: Old climber related to Jacob? (5)

annotation.surface: A question about an old mountaineer who might be a relative of Jacob.
annotation.walkthrough: Jacob looks like the Biblical patriarch; the Jacob is a piebald breed of sheep, so anything related to it is ovine.
annotation.definitionFit: Ovine means relating to sheep, and the Jacob is a sheep breed.

entries.clue: Inconvenience of salary yet to be paid to auditor (9)

indicatorNotes.to auditor: an auditor is a listener, so this is how it strikes the ear

blocks.note: income = salary; owed = yet to be paid

annotation.surface: An auditor is put out by salary that has not been paid.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant checking the books, which suits salary owed; here it just means a listener.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal, rather old-fashioned synonym for putting someone out.

entries.clue: Chicken soup aroused greed? (7)

indicatorNotes.aroused: stirred up, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: greed is one of the deadly sins

annotation.surface: Chicken soup that stirs up an appetite.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chicken soup' reads as one dish, but only 'Chicken' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A poussin is a young chicken raised for eating.

entries.clue: Word that describes central part in English and French (7)

indicatorNotes.in: puts the central part inside the other letters

blocks.note: the pith is the core of a thing

annotation.surface: A grammar note about a word for the middle bit, in both English and French.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And French' is a single unit: the French word for and. Crosswords often borrow tiny foreign words like this, as with LE, DER and UN.
annotation.definitionFit: An epithet is a descriptive word or phrase attached to a name.

entries.clue: Regulator initially blocks licence to supply E (10)

indicatorNotes.initially: takes the first letter of regulator
indicatorNotes.blocks: the R sits inside, blocking the other letters
indicatorNotes.supply: supply as an adverb, supplely: bent into a new shape

annotation.surface: A regulator at first withholds a licence to supply ecstasy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is the adverb from supple, flexibly, and 'E' is the prefix in e-mail and e-commerce, not the drug the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: The E in e-commerce or e-book stands for electronic.

entries.clue: Disneyland’s precisely where spectacles may be seen (2,3,4)

blocks.note: American idiom for exactly; Disneyland stands for the USA
the place a pair of glasses sits on the face

annotation.surface: An exact account of where the shows and parades at Disneyland can be watched.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Disneyland's' marks the first sense as American usage. 'Spectacles' suggests the theme-park shows; it means glasses.
annotation.definitionFit: In American English, on the nose means exactly or precisely; glasses sit on the nose.

entries.clue: High-flier with interest in school fostered by governess (4)

indicatorNotes.fostered by: brought up inside the governess, so the answer lives within that word

blocks.note: the answer sits inside this word, straight after gov-

annotation.surface: A bright pupil, keen on school, is brought up by a governess.
annotation.walkthrough: 'High-flier with interest in school' reads as a star pupil; it is a sea eagle, interested in schools of fish.
annotation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, which hunts fish.

entries.clue: Qualified in final boxing championship (8)

indicatorNotes.boxing: to box something is to enclose it

blocks.note: the final part is the end

annotation.surface: A fighter qualifies for the final of a boxing championship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boxing championship' reads as the sport; 'boxing' is the container instruction, and 'in' only joins definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone qualified for a benefit has the right to it.

entries.clue: American university about to receive fresh opening (8)

indicatorNotes.to receive: the outer letters take the fresh one in

annotation.surface: An American college is about to get a new opening, perhaps a job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About to' looks like 'soon going to'; it splits, RE and then the container indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used especially of a camera's lens opening.

entries.clue: Circulation of trouble-free newspaper led by senior journalist (4)

indicatorNotes.trouble-free: the newspaper is freed of its ail, a trouble

annotation.surface: The editor boosts the circulation of a newspaper untroubled by scandal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Circulation' is a newspaper word in the surface; in the answer it is swirling water.
annotation.definitionFit: An eddy is a circular current in water or air.

entries.clue: Had to take ecstasy to get calmer (3,4)

indicatorNotes.to take: the first letters take the E into themselves

blocks.note: E = ecstasy, the drug; goes inside DID

annotation.surface: Someone had to take a pill to calm down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Had' has to be unpacked as DID OWN; the E then goes into DID to make DIED.
annotation.definitionFit: Wind or excitement that dies down gets calmer.

entries.clue: Take issue with Remain coming to the fore (10)

blocks.note: a point is an issue under discussion

annotation.surface: A voter disputes the Remain campaign's push to the front of the Brexit debate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take issue with' reads as one phrase meaning disagree; the definition is only 'Take', as in your take on things. Remain was the pro-EU side in the 2016 UK referendum.
annotation.definitionFit: Your take on a matter is your standpoint.

entries.clue: Vague legislation no longer supporting case for intervention (7)

indicatorNotes.no longer: ex means former, so a law no longer in force is an ex-act
indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down entry, the legislation sits below and holds up the case
indicatorNotes.case for: the case of a word is its outside letters

annotation.surface: Woolly law, now defunct, used to justify intervening.
annotation.walkthrough: The case for intervention reads as an argument; here it is the word's outer shell, IN.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something not exact is imprecise, hence vague.

entries.clue: What is curbed by supreme command? (6)

indicatorNotes.is curbed by: held in check, so held within the other word

annotation.surface: A question: what is restrained by the highest order?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supreme command' reads as one military term; 'supreme' is the wordplay and 'command' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To act at someone's behest is to act on their command.

entries.clue: Go before pressure leads to really embarrassing surrender (7)

indicatorNotes.leads to: the leading letters of the next words

annotation.surface: Under pressure, someone quits before an embarrassing climbdown.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leads to' looks like 'causes'; it is asking for the first letters of the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from Latin praecedere, to walk in front.

entries.clue: Note head of Greek god captivates heathen (5)

blocks.note: Pan, the Greek god of the wild

annotation.surface: A Greek god enchants an unbeliever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Greek god' reads as one phrase and points straight at Pan; the G is only the head of Greek, and the note and G sit inside him.
annotation.definitionFit: A pagan is a heathen, one outside the main world religions.

entries.clue: Congress backs reckless offer to surrender (7)

indicatorNotes.backs: to back something is to stand behind it, so IT goes at the end
indicatorNotes.reckless: wild, so the letters are thrown about

annotation.surface: Congress supports a rash bid to give in.
annotation.walkthrough: Congress looks like the US legislature and 'backs' like support; congress is sex, IT, and it goes at the back.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with the extra sense of losing something as a penalty.

entries.clue: Whistleblower checking books raised a stink (5)

indicatorNotes.checking: holding back, so holding the books inside
indicatorNotes.raised: in a down entry, raised means read upwards

blocks.note: OT = Old Testament, a set of books

annotation.surface: A whistleblower examining the accounts causes a scandal.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a corporate whistleblower; it is the referee, and the books are the Old Testament. R(OT)EF, read upwards, gives FETOR.
annotation.definitionFit: A fetor is a strong, foul smell.

entries.clue: Plant bottom on silly individual (9)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across entry, one piece comes after the other

blocks.note: a goose is a silly person
the foot is the bottom of a page or hill

annotation.surface: Someone plants their backside on a fool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant bottom on' reads as sitting on someone; 'Plant' is the definition and 'bottom' means foot, not backside.
annotation.definitionFit: Goosefoot is a family of weeds, including fat hen, with leaves shaped like a goose's foot.

entries.clue: Decree this country’s European borders American (5)

indicatorNotes.borders: surrounds, so the American goes inside

blocks.note: a British setter's country is the UK
A = American; goes inside after UK

annotation.surface: A government decree about the UK's European frontier and an American.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This country' is the setter's own, the UK, since The Times is British.
annotation.definitionFit: A ukase was an edict of the Russian tsar, now any arbitrary decree.

entries.clue: Piece played without practice session? (5)

annotation.surface: A match or recital played with no rehearsal.
annotation.walkthrough: A net is a cricket practice session, batting in a netted lane. The musical 'Piece played' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A nonet is a piece of music for nine players.

entries.clue: Makes time to welcome earl demanding serious attention (7)

indicatorNotes.to welcome: the outer letters take the earl in

annotation.surface: Someone finds time to receive a peer on a grave matter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Makes time' reads as finding a moment; here it is two pieces, a verb for earning money and the abbreviation T.
annotation.definitionFit: A dictionary sense: an earnest matter is a grave one, calling for gravity rather than levity.
